newsitem.title: USA: Brazil current account not seen as problem--Malan.
newsitem.headline: Brazil current account not seen as problem--Malan.

text.p: Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan said on Monday that Brazil's current account deficit was not high by international standards and said he foresaw no problems in financing it in 1997 and 1998.
He said the current account deficit rose to 3.3 percent of GDP in 1996 from 2.5 percent of GDP in 1995.
"Three-point-something percentage points of GDP by way of a current account deficit is not high by international standards," Malan said in a speech to the Brazil-U.S. Business Council.
However, growing current account deficits over a period of time may pose some problems, he said.
He said a more important question was how the deficit was financed.
He said 40 percent of Brazil's current account was financed by direct foreign investment last year and increasingly the rest was being financed by longer-term capital.
"So we don't see any problem this year and the next for the financing of (the) current account deficit," he said.

Earlier on Monday, Brazil's central bank said the current account deficit -- the broadest measure of trade -- was $4.584 billion in January and February, up from $1.926 billion in the same period of last year.
Malan said the consensus for Brazilian inflation this year was below seven percent, while he saw real GDP growth at 4.5 percent for the year.
"I see no incompatibility whatsoever between controlling inflation and creating the conditions for sustained growth over time," he said.
Malan added that the government was creating the conditions that hopefully would lead to higher rates of growth in the outer years.
"We have grown at higher rates in the past and we may well grow again at higher rates in the future. We have created the conditions for that," he said.
